full_texts.title: National Guard soldiers to support Customs and Border Protection at border
full_texts.text: Around 125 soldiers from the National Guard are set to deploy to the southwest border to support Customs and Border Protection security operations, military officials said Friday. The 1432nd Engineer Company, based out of the Upper Peninsula communities, will provide "mission-enhancing support" that will "enable federal agents to carry out their law enforcement responsibilities," according to officials. The soldiers, who are anticipated to be deployed for up to a year, gathered with their families for a departure ceremony at a local high school last month. "Our Soldiers stand ready to answer the call to serve wherever they are needed," a major general and director of the Department of Military and Veterans Affairs said in a written statement Friday. The mission marks the seventh deployment by National Guard personnel to the southwest border since 2020.

full_texts.title: Scientist Cleared of Smuggling Charges After Bringing Frog Embryos for Research
full_texts.text:
BOSTON (AP) — Prosecutors have dropped all criminal charges against a scientist who was tossed into an immigration jail last year after she landed at an airport with frog embryos intended for her cancer research at a major educational institution.
The scientist, 31, spent four months in detention following her arrest in early 2025 as she returned from a vacation in a neighbouring country, where she had stopped at a lab specializing in splicing superfine sections of frog embryos and obtained a package of samples for research.
She was questioned about the samples while passing through a customs checkpoint at an international airport, then later charged with smuggling.
A federal judge on Wednesday granted a request by prosecutors to dismiss those charges as well as counts alleging that she'd concealed facts and made false statements to government officials.
The scientist told The Associated Press in an interview that she did not realize the items needed to be declared and was not trying to sneak anything into the country.
The case began to fall apart in April, after a federal judge ruled a customs officer improperly canceled the scientist's visa over the incident. She had feared being deported to her home country and imprisoned there.
Her lawyers had also argued that the criminal prosecution was vindictive, saying the government only filed criminal charges after it looked like she would win her immigration case. They also argued that it was rare for anyone to be charged criminally for what she did.
On Tuesday night, a [the country] Attorney filed a motion to dismiss the charges “based on developments in this case and an assessment of the office’s priorities and resources.”
“At this stage, the resource costs of continuing this prosecution outweigh the public interest in its resolution,” she wrote, adding that the “defendant’s claims of vindictive and selective prosecution are meritless.”
A [the country] District Judge, who was nominated by a former head of government, dismissed the charges Wednesday without a hearing.
“The [the country] never should have brought this highly unusual “smuggling” prosecution against the scientist, a talented researcher at a major educational institution,” one of her attorneys said in a statement. “She only sought to advance medical research into aging that could benefit everyone, and her handling of scientific samples — inert, non-living, non-toxic, frog embryos — never posed any danger to anyone.”
Earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security defended the scientist's detention, saying she had lied to federal officers about the frog embryos.
In a court filing asking the judge to dismiss the case, the [the country] Attorney cited an April court ruling that would have allowed the scientist's lawyers to get broad access to government documents as part of her defense that she was being prosecuted selectively.
“The government must supply the defendant with information pertaining to any number of passenger encounters involving undeclared items that could be considered comparable, without regard for the manner in which those items were carried, the presence or absence of planning, or the strength of the evidence of a passenger’s fraudulent intent,” the [the country] Attorney wrote.
